prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Weekly On-Call Rotation Schedule (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Week 14(Mar 30 – Apr 5)" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Week 15(Apr 6 – 12)" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Week 16(Apr 13 – 19)" spans 1 col × 2 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Week" · longest unbreakable word 40px · one-line width 119px
  col 2: header "Role" · longest unbreakable word 78px · one-line width 78px
  col 3: header "Engineer" · longest unbreakable word 91px · one-line width 129px
  col 4: header "Phone" · longest unbreakable word 46px · one-line width 132px
  col 5: header "Escalation notes" · longest unbreakable word 89px · one-line width 655px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Show who is on call each week, how to reach them, and when escalation or coverage arrangements apply.","reading":"Readers locate a week, distinguish primary from secondary coverage, then scan across for the engineer, phone number, and any action they need to take.","groups":["Week and role establish the schedule hierarchy; each week label serves two role rows.","Engineer and phone form the contact pair for each role.","Escalation notes qualify the contact and coverage information for the same row."],"keep_intact":["Phone numbers, so they can be read and dialed quickly.","Primary and Secondary role labels.","Individual name and date components; engineer names should remain on one line where space permits."],"may_wrap":["Escalation notes can wrap at word boundaries.","Week labels can break between the week number and date range, using the height of their two merged rows.","Engineer names can wrap between given and family names if more space is needed for notes."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r1A: widths [110, 99, 150, 153, 207] · table 720×604px · row heights [36, 106, 83, 106, 83, 83, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1B: widths [95, 99, 135, 153, 237] · table 720×557px · row heights [36, 83, 83, 83, 83, 83, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1C: widths [140, 99, 130, 153, 197] · table 720×697px · row heights [36, 106, 106, 129, 106, 106, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
